h1:
Mae Hong Son Food Guide
Shan, Northern, Yunnan & Cafes
intro: Mae Hong Son eats better than most people expect, because the City of Three Mists sits right where several food cultures meet. Shan cooking that crossed over from Shan State, traditional Northern Thai dishes, Chinese Yunnanese food that put down roots up at Ban Rak Thai, and a new wave of cafes in Pai and around town. The Shan flavors here are mellow rather than fiery, built around backyard greens and tua-nao (fermented soybean) at the heart of everything. We picked the dishes locals actually eat and the shops that are open right now.

blocks.html: To get Mae Hong Son food, you have to start with tua-nao. It's fermented soybean, ground and pressed into thin sheets, then dried. The Shan use it instead of shrimp paste, and it goes into almost every dish — it's what gives the food that rounded, savory aroma you won't find elsewhere. Another thing that sets it apart from the rest of the North: people in Mae Hong Son eat more steamed rice than sticky rice, since sticky rice is saved for making sweets. So most mains come with a bowl of hot steamed rice.

blocks.text: Shan dishes you have to try

blocks.html: This is the real star of the town, and much harder to find elsewhere in Thailand. The easiest place to sample it is the Sai Yud morning market in the center of town. Get there before 7am and you'll find the Shan stalls lined up side by side, so you can graze one dish at a time.

items.name: Tua-nao khao soi (clear-broth khao soi)
items.blurb: Shan khao soi looks nothing like the Chiang Mai version — no coconut milk. It's noodles in a clear broth topped with minced pork stir-fried with tua-nao and tomato, lightly sour and fragrant with fermented soybean, and very easy to put away. A breakfast favorite locals genuinely eat.

items.name: Tofu nu (tou-fu noon)
items.blurb: A thick pea-flour porridge, pale yellow, ladled over noodles or eaten with Burmese-style fried tofu, sprinkled with chili flakes and crispy fried-garlic oil. A hard-to-find breakfast dish that only the northern stalls of the morning market sell.

items.name: Shan hang lay curry
items.blurb: Pork belly simmered with hang lay curry paste and ginger until meltingly tender, balanced sour-salty-sweet. The Shan recipe isn't as thick as the Burmese version. Eat it with hot steamed rice and it's a filling meal.

items.name: Shan jin som + pork crackling
items.blurb: Shan-style soured pork, fried or steamed, eaten with rice or alongside crispy pork crackling. It's a drinking-snack staple and a popular souvenir you can pick up at the markets.

items.name: Khai oop + gaeng kae kai
items.blurb: Khai oop is steamed egg with garden herbs that uses tua-nao instead of shrimp paste, while gaeng kae kai throws a dozen-plus kinds of backyard greens into one pot of chicken curry. A homestyle spread that shows off Shan cooking better than anything.

items.name: Suay tamin, peng mong, ala-wa
items.blurb: Three Shan sweets worth tracking down. Suay tamin is like candied sticky rice, peng mong is fluffy and stringy, and ala-wa adds sago for extra texture. All made from rice flour, coconut milk and cane sugar — fiddly to make, so you won't see them every day.

blocks.title: Morning market tip
blocks.html: The Shan food at Sai Yud market is at its best between 5am and 7am — by mid-morning a lot of stalls have packed up. If you're set on the tofu nu and tua-nao khao soi, get up early to catch them all. And bring cash, because nearly every stall takes cash only.

blocks.text: Yunnanese Chinese food at Ban Rak Thai

blocks.html: Drive up the mountain about an hour and a half from town to reach Ban Rak Thai, a Yunnanese Chinese village beside a reservoir in a mountain valley. The food here is a completely different style from town — known for braised pork hock, fried mantou, and oolong tea grown right on the hillside.

items.name: Pork hock with mantou (Yunnan hot-pot pork hock)
items.blurb: Pork hock braised until it falls apart — clear broth but deep, salty and rich, not sweet like Thai five-spice braises. You eat it with fried mantou that's crisp outside, soft inside and not greasy. The dish everyone who comes up to Ban Rak Thai orders.

items.name: Herbal chicken soup + stir-fried pea shoots
items.blurb: Chicken simmered with Chinese herbs into a broth made naturally sweet by the bones, served with hillside-grown pea shoots stir-fried in garlic oil. Local produce you can only really get up here.

items.name: Home-grown oolong & red tea
items.blurb: Ban Rak Thai grows its own tea, so you can sit and sip hot tea over the reservoir and the mist all day. Well-known spots like Lee Wine Rak Thai have tea-tasting sets to choose from, and you can buy leaves to take home.
items.meta: Ban Rak Thai · Tea set 80–150 THB

blocks.text: Northern Thai and in-town spots where locals go

blocks.html: Beyond the Shan food, the town of Mae Hong Son also has Northern Thai shops and made-to-order places where locals actually eat. Here are the ones worth a try.

items.name: Khao Soi Pa Nuan
items.blurb: A khao soi shop that's been part of the town for decades, with several styles to choose from, around 50 THB a bowl. It's small but packs out at lunch.

items.name: Kai Mook
items.blurb: On Khunlumprapas Road, serving Central Thai food with a Shan accent at good prices. A dinner spot where locals and travelers tend to meet up.

items.name: Salween River Restaurant
items.blurb: An old shop by Nong Chong Kham lake in the center of town, serving Shan food alongside Western dishes like pasta and pizza. Good for lingering over a drink with a lakeside view.

items: Sai Yud market (morning market) — the hub for Shan food: tua-nao khao soi, tofu nu, local sweets, all in one place. Open from before dawn.
Mae Hong Son walking street — by Nong Chong Kham lake; in the evening, rows of street-food and snack stalls, with the temple's chedi reflected in the water after dark.
Pai walking street — for the Pai crowd; come evening the whole street turns into a food run of savory and sweet bites, easy to graze your way full.

blocks.html: On the cafe front, the busiest scene is in Pai, with mountain-view coffee shops scattered the whole way along the road. In the town of Mae Hong Son itself, there are little cafes by Nong Chong Kham lake to sit and relax.

items.name: Coffee in Love (Pai)
items.blurb: A yellow-house cafe on the highway just before you reach Pai, with a terrace looking out over the whole valley. A popular photo spot; drinks start around 50 THB, open daily morning to evening.

items.name: Nong Chong Kham lakeside cafes
items.blurb: In town there are little cafes around Nong Chong Kham lake — sit with a coffee and watch the chedi of Wat Chong Kham and Wat Chong Klang over the morning mist.

items.name: Ban Rak Thai tea houses
items.blurb: If you'd rather skip coffee, head up to Ban Rak Thai for hot oolong by the reservoir — a natural cafe setting that feels almost like being abroad.

blocks.title: Edible souvenirs
blocks.html: The edible souvenirs people like to bring back are oolong tea leaves from Ban Rak Thai, sheets of tua-nao, sesame brittle, and Shan sweets like suay tamin and ala-wa. Pai, meanwhile, has plenty of cookie and sesame-sheet souvenirs — pick whatever's on your route.

faq.q: What food do you have to try in Mae Hong Son?
faq.a: Top of the list are tua-nao khao soi (the clear-broth Shan khao soi with no coconut milk), tofu nu, and Shan hang lay curry. If you head up to Ban Rak Thai, try the Yunnan pork hock with mantou and the home-grown oolong tea. Finish with Shan sweets like suay tamin, peng mong and ala-wa.

faq.q: How is Shan food different from regular Northern Thai food?
faq.a: Shan food is mellow rather than fiery, leaning on backyard greens and using tua-nao (dried fermented soybean) instead of shrimp paste as the heart of its flavor. People in Mae Hong Son eat more steamed rice than sticky rice, and Shan khao soi is a clear broth with no coconut milk — unlike the coconut-milk khao soi of Chiang Mai.

faq.q: Where can you eat authentic Shan food in Mae Hong Son?
faq.a: The easiest spot is the Sai Yud morning market in the center of town. Get there before 7am and you'll find the Shan stalls lined up — tua-nao khao soi, tofu nu at the northern stalls, and local sweets. Bring cash, since most stalls only take cash.

faq.q: What's good to eat at Ban Rak Thai, and how far is it from town?
faq.a: Ban Rak Thai is about an hour and a half from town by car. The dishes to order are Yunnan pork hock with mantou, herbal chicken soup, and stir-fried hillside-grown pea shoots, finished with hot oolong tea overlooking the reservoir. A well-known shop in the village is Lee Wine Rak Thai.

faq.q: Where can you find good cafes around Mae Hong Son?
faq.a: The liveliest cafe scene is in Pai, with mountain-view shops lined up the whole way along the road — well-known ones like Coffee in Love, the yellow house just before you reach Pai. In the town itself there are little cafes around Nong Chong Kham lake where you can sit and watch the chedi over the morning mist.
